It discusses how each layer type stores and recalls key-value pairs, with self-attention offering significantly higher memory capacity and recall accuracy compared to simpler layers. The piece uses the concept of interference-to-signal ratio to measure memory capacity and illustrates how self-attention can store over a million memories with 64-dimensional keys, far surpassing linear layers and MLPs. The analysis provides an intuitive framework for understanding the memory capabilities underlying large language models and their ability to recall vast amounts of information.

items.title: PS5LM enables jailbroken PS5 consoles to run llama.cpp with GGUF models natively on the GPU, serving language and decision models over the network [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Llama.cpp on a jailbroken PS5: run any GGUF model natively on the console
items.summary:
PS5LM is a homebrew application that allows jailbroken PlayStation 5 consoles to run language models using llama.cpp on the console's RDNA 2 GPU. It supports loading GGUF models and serves them via OpenAI and Anthropic-compatible APIs to devices on the local network, without needing a PC or cloud service. The app also supports decision models powered by Ollaya, which provide typed decisions with calibrated probabilities in real time.

The software uses Vulkan backend and allocates 11.4 GB of shared memory for models and context, displaying interactions on the TV screen and monitoring system metrics like temperature and GPU load. Users can download models directly to the console's internal or external storage and interact with the models through browsers or compatible clients. PS5LM requires a jailbroken PS5 running firmware versions 7.00 to 13.60 and is open source under GPL-3.0-or-later, with no affiliation to Sony Interactive Entertainment.

items.title: Apple ML Research releases MLX for local and distributed large language model inference on Mac Studio, enabling Muse Spark Open with nearly a trillion parameters [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio
items.summary:
Apple ML Research has introduced MLX, an open-source framework that allows AI researchers and developers to run large language models locally and across multiple Mac Studios using Apple silicon. The framework leverages unified memory architecture and supports models like Muse Spark Open, which has nearly a trillion parameters and can generate over 36 tokens per second on a cluster of four Mac Studios. MLX supports both single-device and distributed inference with RDMA over Thunderbolt, optimizing performance and energy efficiency on Mac Studio hardware.

The research benchmarks several models including Muse Spark Open, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Qwen 3.8 on Mac Studio with M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra chips, highlighting significant speedups in time to first token and generation throughput due to the M5 Ultra's GPU Neural Accelerator and increased memory bandwidth. The Mac Studio maintains modest power consumption, making it suitable for AI workloads in typical office or home environments. Muse Spark Open's large memory requirements are addressed through 4-bit quantization, enabling its deployment across multiple Mac Studios.

items.title: BFL releases FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation and editing with native 4K support and multi-reference input [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FLUX 3 Image Klein
items.summary:
BFL has launched FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6 billion parameter open weights model designed for text-to-image generation, image editing, and multi-reference generation using up to 10 reference images. The model supports native 4K image generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding box controls to specify element placement or restrict edits. It builds on FLUX 3's multimodal learning from images, video, and audio to produce realistic images grounded in real-world dynamics.

FLUX 3 Image Klein is optimized for consumer GPUs, requiring less memory and enabling local deployment and on-device editing. It outperforms larger open and some closed models in internal evaluations for text-to-image and image editing tasks while being smaller and faster. The release includes base and distilled models with FP8, INT8, and NVFP4 builds supported by NVIDIA, available under the FLUX Kommunity License for free commercial use by smaller organizations and research. The model is accessible via the BFL API, Hugging Face, and supports fine-tuning with popular toolkits.

items.title: Decompilation community faces conflict as AI tools accelerate game code reverse engineering and clout chasing increases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Decompilations, AI, and the Chase for Clout
items.summary:
The decompilation community, which works to reverse engineer and preserve game source code, is experiencing turmoil due to the rise of AI tools that can convert assembly code into C/C++ code more quickly. This has led to increased competition, code theft accusations, and the shutdown of a progress-tracking website, with some community members criticizing the rush for fame over quality and collaboration.

Josh, an experienced decompiler involved in projects like LEGO Island and Mario Kart 64, explains that while AI has sped up parts of the process, high-quality decompilation still requires significant manual effort to ensure accuracy and maintain the integrity of the codebase. The community is grappling with misunderstandings about decompilation versus porting and recompilation, as well as challenges around respecting contribution guidelines and managing open repositories.

The situation highlights tensions between traditional decompilation practices and new AI-driven approaches, raising questions about how the community can balance innovation, collaboration, and recognition while preserving the technical and historical value of game code.

items.originalTitle: He Wants AI Benchmarking to Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
items.summary:
Moritz Hardt, a computer scientist and director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, argues that AI benchmarking has been fundamentally broken for decades, yet it has inadvertently driven progress in machine learning. He highlights how benchmarks have shaped AI development, from causing an AI winter in the late 1980s to sparking the deep learning revolution in the 2010s, but now face challenges with large language models like GPT-6 Astra.

Hardt explains that benchmarks, which rank AI models based on standardized tests, have become more like competitions where models can game the system rather than truly demonstrate intelligence. He emphasizes the need for a more rigorous, scientific approach to benchmarking that avoids overfitting to test sets and promotes transparency, aiming to restore credibility and better measure AI capabilities in the evolving landscape.

items.originalTitle: Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed
items.summary:
Meta has launched Muse Spark Open, an 816 billion parameter open-weight AI model designed for coding and agentic tasks with a 1 million token context window. This release marks a significant step forward for American open-weight models, narrowing the performance gap with leading Chinese models and revitalizing the Western open AI ecosystem. Muse Spark Open includes additional safety training and is intended to be deployed with system guardrails due to its restrictive license terms.

The model's license requires users to display "Built with Muse" branding, imposes revenue-based licensing for companies earning over $20 million monthly, and enforces an acceptable use policy, making it less open than typical open-source models. This release comes amid competitive pressure from other labs like Reflection and Mistral, which have announced strong models but have yet to release weights. Meta's move reasserts its leadership in the frontier AI model space and influences the dynamics of open AI development in the West.

items.originalSummary:
Welcome, Weekenders!

A song has been stuck on loop in my mind for days now. Yeah, this one. 

C’mon, haven’t you heard the big, brassy James Bond theme playing too? We have an honest-to-goodness spy scandal on our hands! That would be the affair over at OpenAI, where the FBI has arrested a former engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, for allegedly placing a toilet paper–wrapped recording device in a conference room. Why’d he do it? The Justice Department wasn’t explicit in its press release announcing Alfozan’s arrest, though the statement does make sure to prominently describe him as a “national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” implying, obviously, that he was hoping to spy on OpenAI for the Saudis.

I expect a not unsizable part of Silicon Valley experienced some schadenfreude when reading about the turn of events at OpenAI. I’d advise against indulging in that feeling, because when I struck up conversations with a few corporate security consultants and surveillance experts over the last few days, they all echoed the same sentiment: Plenty of companies risk ending up in the same situation—especially as they move quickly in today’s era of frenzied, heightened competition. A discomforting thought, eh?

“Organizations can sometimes be moving so fast that they often don’t understand that there’s an issue associated with somebody until that person’s on board and up to no good,” said Bill Priestap, a former head of FBI counterintelligence who now runs his own security consultancy, Trenchcoat Advisors. “Meaning they’re recruiting, and they’re under such pressure to get the right people and get them on board that in many regards, they end up with a minimal understanding of the people they’re bringing on board.” Well, good thing there hasn’t been an enormous, frantic hiring binge lately. Ha ha ha. 

If you’re starting to feel a little paranoid, I strongly, strongly advise against talking to someone like David Abbott, a San Francisco private detective, to find out how easy it is to bug an office. Such conversations will only further unnerve you—you might end up holding your next board meeting in your home basement, Tony Soprano style—because according to Abbott, it’s pretty darn easy to install a recording device. 

A suitable one can be bought for less than $100. Some of the popular ones resemble phone chargers, which get tucked into a power socket, hidden in plain sight. He’s also seen surveillance devices in fake coffee cups—you know, like the ones that might lie casually around an office—and quite a few in fake smoke alarms. 

More bad news: Should you find such a device, it’s like spotting an ant in your kitchen. One ant suggests the presence of more ants. “If I’m doing a bug sweep, just because I find one does not mean there isn’t a second,” said Abbott. “If you find one, there’s going to be two. If you find two, there’s going to be three. You just keep looking.”

What happened at OpenAI underscores Abbott’s warning. There, Alfozan, the alleged spy, did plant two bugs. Well, he tried to do so. Alfozan, not the sort who seems like he would’ve ever earned double 0 status, had placed another bug in a bag that he then mislaid: He reported it missing and had to go pick it up from the company’s lost and found.

OK, if I’ve spooked the heck out of you, I guess I can offer some solace by pointing you in the direction of Eric and Greg Levesque, whose Salt Lake City–based startup, Strider Technologies, has raised $110 million in the last few years to sell AI-powered software to businesses that monitors email and other internal communications, flagging suspicious behavior and possible espionage attempts. (Yes, the company’s name is a reference to Strider from “The Lord of the Rings,” the nom de cloak of Aragorn, the character Viggo Mortensen plays.) 

“What we’ve found is that companies are not always dealing with trained intelligence operatives. Like, they’re dealing with scientists or legitimate engineers who have been approached or coerced in some form or fashion and are now working on behalf of someone else,” said Greg Levesque. “They can leave a lot of digital exhaust.”—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

As the pandemic shut down the world in 2020, Sayre Quevedo, then a producer for The New York Times’ “The Daily” podcast, quit his job and headed out to Los Angeles, hoping for a chance at self-reinvention. To cope with those tumultuous times, he decided to pursue a documentary project, recording every phone call. Had nothing else of import happened in his life, Quevedo might’ve wound up with an intriguing time capsule. But something quite unusual did occur: Just months after moving to LA, he and his twin brother, Connor, happened to finally locate their biological father, whom they’d never before met. He worked as a barber—blocks from where Sayre lived. “Reaching Out,” a new podcast co-produced by NPR station KCRW that won a top prize in the Tribeca Festival’s expanded podcast categories, is a starkly intimate account of their journey to meet him and their reconciliation with each other, their lives and what life might’ve been like if their father hadn’t been a total stranger who happened to be just down the street.—Abram Brown

Reading: “Sitcom” by Chuck Lorre and “Emperor of Nothing” by Blake J. Harris

Chuck Lorre, the indefatigable TV showrunner, writer and producer, has kept the masses laughing for years—and years—and years, with a list of hits that includes “Two and a Half Men,” “The Big Bang Theory” and “Dharma and Greg.” Those are sitcoms, a term Lorre acknowledges once made him practically break out in hives, since it was often used to cheapen what he sees as grueling, high-touch art. With spicy good humor, he reclaims the word in his new memoir about his time in Hollywood, “Sitcom.” 

“The truth is, making a live studio audience laugh for twenty-odd minutes every week, for twenty-two weeks, is incredibly hard and unbelievably stressful,” Lorre writes. “If you’re one of those people who insist on labeling all sitcoms as being cheap, juvenile and unsophisticated, well...all I can say is, blow me.”

I’d say “Sitcom” functions as a good primer on managing talent, too, and Lorre attests to having learned the importance of keeping out of the way. “Creativity needs air to breathe,” he writes. To do the opposite risks turning a leader into “one of those plastic bags you get at the dry cleaners that can kill small children.” Lorre also takes the opportunity to set down what he sees as good comedy’s basic tenets and decry the medium’s basest impulse: to write only about stupid people doing stupid things: “A better, perhaps deeper means to achieving laughter involves pain and suffering.”

Such a sentiment is most certainly shared by Larry David of “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” the subject of “Emperor of Nothing,” a biography that won his reluctant cooperation. (When author Blake J. Harris finally wore David down, Harris received a two-line email from him: “Oh Jesus. If we must.”) As with “Sitcom,” “Emperor of Nothing” charts a remarkable rise across Hollywood from an inauspicious start: Lorre was a wannabe musician before his TV run, while David was a little-known stand-up comic with an unremarkable series of TV writing jobs before co-creating “Seinfeld.”

Like Lorre, David describes the process of penning comedy as an arduous affair. And by David’s own telling, the process of sitting down to write a new “Seinfeld” season would bring on full panic. “That always seemed like a daunting prospect,” he recalled. “Especially because all the good ideas were used up the year before.” Fortunately, David had his friendship with the show’s eponymous star, Jerry Seinfeld, one of many people within David’s orbit who gave interviews for “Emperor of Nothing.” “I would always say, ‘All we have to do is write today,’” Seinfeld said. Or as David recalled: “Jerry always talked me off the ledge.”—A.B.

Watching: “War”

No one does a charming, self-involved cad better than Dominic West, the British character actor who first washed ashore in America as “The Wire”’s Detective McNulty and then again in Showtime’s “The Affair” and in the final two seasons of “The Crown” as Prince Charles. In “War,” HBO’s new high-tension legal drama, he’s tech billionaire Morgan Henderson, a fellow championing a safer, more responsible social media—while embroiled in an increasingly messy divorce from his Hollywood star wife, Carla (Sienna Miller). Much of that mess is Morgan’s own doing: He looks wonderful in his Savile Row trousers—he just has trouble keeping them on. As Morgan and Carla gird for an extended battle, they assemble a posse of cutthroat attorneys, who find their impulsive clients constantly upending their carefully laid strategies. That flock of legal eagles includes a handsome rogue, Johnny (Archie Renaux), a lad from working-class south London who sees a chance to ascend by, uh, redefining zealous representation. Backstabbing and double crosses abound.—A.B.

items.originalTitle: Anthropics' Claude cracks a 25-year-old NSA cryptography mystery in under 30 minutes
items.summary:
Anthropic's AI model Claude resolved a 25-year-old cryptography puzzle involving the unexplained seeds behind NIST's standard curves for digital signatures, which were originally provided by the NSA. Claude determined in under 30 minutes that the seeds were generated using "lrand48," a basic C random number generator initialized with a Unix timestamp, reducing suspicion of deliberate backdoors.

The NSA had supplied these seeds without explanation when NIST standardized elliptic-curve digital signature algorithm (ECDSA) curves around 2000, leading to long-standing speculation about potential backdoors. Claude's discovery, based on the pattern of 31-bit outputs and zeroed top bits in some seeds, suggests the seeds were not maliciously crafted. Anthropic is donating the $36,864 bounty for solving the mystery to the Internet Security Research Group.

items.title: Basis.ai demonstrates LLMs verifying programming language semantics by proving interpreter correctness against compiled RISC-V code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Ship Your Interpreter
items.summary:
Basis.ai reports an experiment where large language models (LLMs) developed a formal semantics and proof for a small programming language by verifying that the semantics agree with the behavior of its interpreter compiled to RISC-V machine code. This approach treats the compiled interpreter as ground truth, enabling formal verification of language semantics, which is a key bottleneck in scaling verified software development.

The experiment used an extended version of the WHILE language and employed the Lean proof assistant to prove that the semantics rules predict exactly the interpreter's behavior for every program. This method addresses challenges in creating formal semantics for languages without existing formal definitions and aims to improve software security by enabling verified software that keeps pace with evolving AI-assisted attacks.

Basis.ai's work highlights the shift in verification challenges from theorem proving to specification accuracy and suggests that verifying semantics against interpreters could scale formal verification efforts to more complex software systems.
